For owners of aging hydropower assets, this represents a substantial increase in the potential unplanned downtime that could be caused by the failure of an LPT. For LPTs that are already at or beyond their design lifetime, longer lead times are especially challenging because the failure rate increases with the age of the unit (Tenbohlen, Hanif, and Martin n.d.). The process of procuring a replacement for an LPT nearing the end of its service life may need to begin sooner to account for longer lead times. Since current lead times for LPTs are stretching up to four years, procurement activities could begin years in advance, rather than months or weeks. Domestic transformer manufacturers highlighted some critical transformer components that have very long lead times and limited domestic supply. Bushings for LPTs are currently the item with the longest lead time, up to 130 weeks. OLTCs take 80–90 weeks to procure and have just 1 or 2 U.S. manufacturers; otherwise, they are typically sourced from Europe. One domestic transformer manufacturer said they order extra inventory ahead of time or ask customers to be open to different makes or specifications for a particular product to address the long lead times for OLTCs and bushings. Pressboard is another critical item with a single domestic manufacturer and is often imported as well. Sourcing pressboard is a global challenge, except perhaps from China. LPT costs: Transformer costs have increased sharply since 2021, with prices in 2025 approximately 80% higher than the relatively constant value between 2014 and 2021 (Figure 8). Due to high levels of import dependence for both finished LPTs and components and materials used in domestic LPT production, increased tariff rates will likely result in higher costs. Figure 8. With a great proportion of the hydropower engineering workforce nearing 16 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. retirement age, the niche expertise to design generator step-up units for hydroelectric plants, which are typically made to custom standards, is in a critical condition. A 2020 U.S. Department of Commerce survey reports that 89% of American companies that manufacture components struggle to find qualified workers (U.S. Department of Energy 2024). This notion is further supported by interviews conducted with manufacturers and vendors of hydropower components who noted shortages of workers with more than 10 years of experience in the industry. Many of these workers are moving to other industries due to wage differences.
